dok_rationale: Part (c) judges two headlines by relating the graph baseline to visible bar heights and contrasting that impression with the actual counts.
stem: Suppose 184 students chose a favorite lunch option. A newsletter printed \textbf{Graph A} with the headline ``\textbf{Pizza wins by a landslide.}'' A council member redrew the data as \textbf{Graph B} and said, ``It is basically a tie.''
first_take: Is pizza clearly the favorite? Name the graph that most influenced you.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Read the Pizza and Pasta counts. How many more students chose Pizza?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Graph A starts at 40. Find the visible heights above 40 for Pizza and Pasta. Compare those heights with the actual counts.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which graph gives a fairer picture of the lunch votes? Explain how its scale affects the comparison. Use your counts to judge both `landslide' and `basically a tie,' then write a more accurate headline.

answers.a: Pizza has 52 students and Pasta 41, so Pizza has 11 more.
answers.b: Visible heights: Pizza 52-40=12 and Pasta 41-40=1. Pizza looks 12 times as tall, while the actual counts are 52 and 41, a difference of 11 students.
answers.c: Graph B uses zero, so full bar heights represent counts. Graph A starts at 40 and exaggerates the difference: visible heights are 12 to 1, but counts are 52 to 41. Pizza has the most votes, yet neither a huge landslide nor an exact tie describes the counts. A supported headline is `Pizza leads Pasta by 11 votes; all four options receive support.' Accept other measured wording supported by the counts.

expectedElements.description: Chooses B and explains zero baseline makes heights proportional to counts
Contrasts Graph A's 12-to-1 visible heights with 52 versus 41 or an 11-vote difference
Judges both headlines and supplies a bounded headline supported by the counts

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: Calling Graph A's counts false instead of explaining its baseline
Treating the visible heights as vote counts
Repeating a headline without using the counts
